title: Performance anti-patterns
scopeHtml: Scope: N+1, chatty services, thundering herd, unbounded queues, lock contention, GC pauses, other anti-patterns. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why anti-patterns matter
notes.html:
A performance anti-pattern is a common design mistake that works fine in a demo and collapses under real load. Most production slowdowns are not exotic; they are a handful of repeating shapes. Learning to spot them in a design or a code review is a core senior skill.

Method for any slowness:

  1. Measure first (p50/p99 latency, throughput, CPU, memory, GC, DB time, queue depth). Do not guess.
  2. Find the bottleneck resource (USE method): CPU, memory, disk, network, locks, connection pool.
  3. Fix the cheapest big thing, measure again.

Amdahl's law reminder: if 90% of the time is in the database, making the app code 10x faster improves overall time by only about 8%.

The anti-patterns below: N+1 queries, chatty services, thundering herd (and cache stampede), unbounded queues and unbounded everything, lock contention, GC pauses, plus a short list of others.

Industry examples. Facebook's memcache paper described leases to stop thundering herds; Twitter's early Rails "fail whale" era was partly N+1 and queue problems; Discord moved a hot service from Go to Rust partly due to garbage-collection latency spikes every couple of minutes (their public write-up); LinkedIn and Netflix tuned JVM GC extensively.

Everyday analogy. A traffic jam usually has one cause (a narrow bridge); widening every other road does not help.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising without measuring.
  • Fixing symptoms (add more servers) when a code-level pattern is the cause.

notes.title: N+1 queries
notes.html:
The N+1 problem: 1 query fetches a list of N items, then N more queries fetch each item's related data one by one. Total N+1 round trips instead of 1 or 2.

// Looks innocent: 1 query for orders + N queries for each order's customer
val orders = orderRepo.findAll()                      // 1 query (say 100 rows)
orders.forEach { o -> println(o.customer.name) }      // lazy load: 100 more queries

Why it hurts. Each query costs a network round trip (0.3 to 1 ms in-region) plus parsing and planning. 100 orders -> 101 queries -> 30 to 100 ms; 10,000 rows -> over 5 seconds, and it multiplies DB load at scale: 1,000 req/s x 101 queries = 101,000 queries/s, which can saturate the database.

Fixes:

  • Join / join fetch: one query: SELECT ... FROM orders JOIN customers. JPA: JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.
  • Batch fetch (IN query): SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (...), 2 queries total; Hibernate @BatchSize, or Rails includes/preload, Django select_related / prefetch_related.
  • DataLoader (GraphQL): batches and caches per-request loads (Facebook's DataLoader).
  • Denormalise or cache rarely-changing related data.
  • Android Room: use @Relation with @Transaction rather than querying inside a loop.
-- 1 query instead of 101
SELECT o.id, o.total, c.name
FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.created_at > now() - interval '1 day';

-- or 2 queries
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE ...;
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (7, 9, 12, 15);

Detection. Log or count SQL statements per request (Hibernate statistics, pg_stat_statements showing one query with huge call counts and tiny mean time), APM traces showing hundreds of identical sibling DB spans, tests that assert query counts (Django assertNumQueries).

Trade-offs. A big join can return duplicated parent data (one-to-many cartesian explosion): use batched IN queries or fetch separately. Over-fetching columns also costs memory.

Decision gravity. Easy to fix locally and reversible; the real fix is a team habit: query-count assertions in tests and ORM lazy-loading awareness.

Industry examples. GitHub's GraphQL API and Shopify use DataLoader-style batching; Rails's Bullet gem flags N+1; Hibernate lazy loading is the classic cause.

Everyday analogy. Going to the supermarket 100 times to buy 100 items instead of making one trip with a list.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing an ORM makes this go away.
  • "Fixing" it with a huge join that returns millions of duplicated rows.
  • Not checking the SQL the ORM actually generated.

notes.title: Chatty services
notes.html:
A chatty service makes many small remote calls to do one job. Each call adds latency (network RTT plus serialization) and failure probability.

In-process call: nanoseconds. Cross-service call in the same datacenter: about 0.5 to 2 ms plus the callee's time. Calls multiply: a page that makes 40 sequential calls of 5 ms each is 200 ms before any logic.

Availability also multiplies: 40 calls each 99.9% -> 0.999^40 = 96%.

Fixes:

  • Batching: one call with a list of IDs instead of N calls (GET /users?ids=1,2,3).
  • Parallelise independent calls (async/await, coroutines async), so latency is the max not the sum.
  • Coarser-grained APIs: return what the screen needs (BFF: Backend For Frontend, GraphQL, or an aggregated endpoint).
  • Caching stable data near the caller.
  • Co-locate tightly coupled logic (merge services if two always change and scale together; the "distributed monolith" smell).
  • Use async messaging for work that does not need a response.
  • Efficient protocols: gRPC/protobuf and HTTP/2 multiplexing, keep-alive connections.
// Kotlin: independent calls in parallel -> latency = max(a,b,c), not a+b+c
suspend fun home(userId: String) = coroutineScope {
    val profile = async { profileApi.get(userId) }
    val orders  = async { orderApi.recent(userId) }
    val recs    = async { recsApi.forUser(userId) }
    HomeScreen(profile.await(), orders.await(), recs.await())
}

Worked example. Mobile home screen: 12 sequential REST calls at 80 ms (mobile network RTT) = 960 ms plus TLS handshakes if not reused. A BFF that fans out in parallel in the datacenter (12 calls at 3 ms, in parallel, about 10 ms) returns one response in about 100 ms total to the phone. Mobile benefits hugely because the expensive hop is the radio link.

Industry examples. Netflix's API gateway/BFF and later GraphQL federation reduce device round trips; Amazon's famous page assembled from many services with strict per-call latency budgets; Uber reorganised from thousands of microservices toward domain-oriented boundaries (DOMA) partly to reduce chatty dependencies; Amazon Prime Video moved a monitoring pipeline from microservices to a monolith and cut cost by 90% (their 2023 write-up).

Decision gravity. Service boundaries are close to one-way doors: merging or splitting services is expensive. Draw boundaries along data ownership and change cadence so that typical operations stay within one service.

Everyday analogy. Asking a colleague 20 separate one-line questions by email instead of sending one message with all 20.

Common interview traps.

  • Sequential calls that could be parallel.
  • Calling a service in a loop (the N+1 problem across the network).
  • Splitting into microservices without considering call graphs.

notes.title: Thundering herd and cache stampede
notes.html:
A thundering herd is many clients or threads reacting to the same event at the same instant, overwhelming a shared resource. Typical triggers: a popular cache key expires, a service restarts, a lock is released, a cron fires at :00, a push notification wakes millions of devices.

Cache stampede (dogpile). A hot key expires; 5,000 requests/s all miss at once and all hit the database to recompute it. The DB, sized for a 95% cache hit rate, suddenly gets 100% of traffic and falls over, which in turn keeps the cache from refilling.

Fixes:

  1. Request coalescing / single flight: only one request recomputes; others wait for its result (Go singleflight, Guava LoadingCache, Caffeine refreshAfterWrite).
  2. Distributed lock or lease on the key (Facebook memcache "leases": one client gets a lease to refill; others wait or get a slightly stale value).
  3. Stale-while-revalidate / serve stale on error: keep returning the old value while one refresher updates it in the background.
  4. TTL jitter: TTL = 300 s + random(0, 60 s) so many keys do not expire together.
  5. Probabilistic early refresh (XFetch): refresh with increasing probability as expiry approaches.
  6. Pre-warming caches before taking traffic after a deploy or failover.
  7. Never expire extremely hot keys, refresh them by a background job.
import random, time

def ttl_with_jitter(base=300, spread=60):
    return base + random.uniform(0, spread)       # avoid synchronised expiry

# Single-flight idea: first caller computes, others wait on the same future
inflight = {}
def get(key):
    v = cache.get(key)
    if v is not None:
        return v
    fut = inflight.setdefault(key, new_future())   # only the first creates the work
    if fut.is_new:
        fut.set(recompute(key)); cache.set(key, fut.value, ttl_with_jitter())
    return fut.wait()

Other herds.

  • Retry storms after an outage (use backoff and jitter).
  • Reconnect storms: a WebSocket gateway restarts and 2M mobile clients reconnect in seconds. Use randomised reconnect delays, connection rate limits and gradual rollouts.
  • Cron at midnight: spread schedules with jitter. Android WorkManager and Firebase push both batch and jitter to avoid server spikes.
  • Cold start after failover: empty caches mean 100% misses.

Worked example. Key with 10,000 req/s, DB recompute takes 200 ms. Without coalescing, during those 200 ms about 2,000 requests each run the expensive query. With single flight, exactly 1 query runs and 1,999 requests share the result.

Industry examples. Facebook's memcache leases (NSDI 2013 paper); Cloudflare and Fastly "request collapsing" to the origin; Varnish grace mode; Netflix EVCache; Instagram.

Decision gravity. Cheap to add early (jitter, single flight) and reversible; painful to discover during an outage. Stale-serving is a product decision: which data may be stale and for how long.

Everyday analogy. The shop opens its doors at 9:00 on sale day and everyone rushes the one till; staggered entry or several tills fixes it.

Common interview traps.

  • All keys sharing the same TTL.
  • Fixing the cache stampede but leaving retry storms and reconnect storms.
  • Not warming caches on a new region or after a flush.

notes.title: Unbounded queues and unbounded everything
notes.html:
Anything without a limit will eventually grow until it breaks something else. Unbounded queues, thread pools, caches, result sets, retries, request sizes and connection counts.

The unbounded queue. When arrival rate > service rate, a queue absorbs the difference only while memory lasts. Latency becomes (queue length / service rate): a backlog of 600,000 items at 1,000 items/s means 10 minutes wait, so every request is already stale and users have retried. Then OOM kills the process and the queue is lost.

Classic traps:

  • Java Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue; newCachedThreadPool has unbounded threads. Create ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and a rejection policy (CallerRunsPolicy applies backpressure).
  • Unbounded in-memory caches (HashMap as cache): use Caffeine with maximumSize and TTL.
  • SELECT * without LIMIT/pagination loading millions of rows into memory.
  • Unbounded retry loops and log volume (disk fills).
  • Unbounded per-tenant usage (no quotas): one tenant starves others.
  • Android: unbounded in-memory bitmap caches cause OOM; use LruCache sized as a fraction of heap.
// Bounded pool: 16 threads, queue of 200, caller runs when full (natural backpressure)
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16, 0L, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(200),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

Worked example. Queue holds 1 KB messages. A 30-minute overload at +2,000 msg/s net adds 3.6M messages = 3.6 GB, enough to crash a 4 GB heap. With a bound of 10,000 messages (10 MB) the system rejects the excess immediately and stays alive.

Little's law check. In-flight items = arrival rate x time in system. 1,000 req/s at 2 s latency means 2,000 concurrent requests holding resources; if latency rises to 20 s this becomes 20,000: memory and threads explode. Bound concurrency, and monitor queue depth and queue wait time.

Choose the overflow policy explicitly: block producers, reject (503), drop oldest/newest (telemetry), or spill to durable storage (Kafka, SQS).

Industry examples. Many JVM incidents trace back to newFixedThreadPool; Kafka and SQS act as durable bounded-by-disk buffers with lag alerts; Netflix concurrency limits; Slack's 2021 outage retrospectives mention overload and scaling limits (confirm details in their post-mortems).

Decision gravity. Choosing bounds and overflow behaviour is a design-time decision, easy to change, but defaults are dangerous. Persistent queues change durability guarantees (at-least-once, ordering).

Everyday analogy. A bathtub with the tap on full and a drain that is too small: without an overflow outlet, it floods the house.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "add a queue" to absorb load without bounding it.
  • Using default executors.
  • Monitoring CPU but not queue depth/age.

notes.title: Lock contention
notes.html:
Lock contention is threads spending their time waiting for a lock instead of working. Adding CPUs or threads makes it no faster, sometimes slower.

Symptoms: low CPU utilisation but poor throughput and high latency; thread dumps show many threads BLOCKED or WAITING on the same monitor; throughput plateaus as you add threads. In databases: lock waits (pg_locks with granted = false), row-lock hot spots, deadlocks.

Amdahl: if 10% of the work happens inside one global lock (serial), the maximum speed-up is 1 / 0.10 = 10x, no matter how many cores.

Fixes:

  • Shorten the critical section: do I/O, logging and computation outside the lock.
  • Reduce granularity: per-key/striped locks (ConcurrentHashMap locks per bin / CAS), sharded counters (LongAdder rather than a single AtomicLong under heavy contention).
  • Lock-free / immutable data: copy-on-write for read-mostly data (CopyOnWriteArrayList), ReadWriteLock / StampedLock when reads dominate.
  • Avoid lock ordering deadlocks: always acquire in a consistent order, use tryLock with timeout.
  • Message passing / single writer: one thread owns the data (actor model, LMAX Disruptor, Kotlin channels), eliminating locks.
  • Database hot rows: counter on one row updated by every request. Fix with sharded counters (N rows, sum on read), batching/aggregation in memory, INSERT event rows and aggregate later, or Redis INCR. Keep transactions short; take locks in the same order; SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED for queues.
// Bad: synchronized around a slow call
@Synchronized fun update(x: Item) { db.save(x); cache.put(x.id, x) }   // db.save under the lock

// Better: do slow work outside, lock only the tiny shared update
fun update(x: Item) { db.save(x); synchronized(lock) { cache[x.id] = x } }
-- Hot row: every order updates one counter row (serialises all writers)
UPDATE stats SET orders = orders + 1 WHERE id = 1;
-- Sharded: pick random slot of 16; sum on read
UPDATE stats_sharded SET orders = orders + 1 WHERE id = floor(random()*16);

Worked example. A service guards a map with one synchronized block that takes 2 ms (includes a log call). Max throughput = 1 / 0.002 = 500 ops/s, regardless of 32 cores. Moving logging out (0.05 ms inside the lock) gives 20,000 ops/s.

Diagnosis tools. JVM: thread dumps (jstack, 3 dumps 5 s apart), async-profiler lock mode, JFR lock profiling; Linux perf, off-CPU flame graphs; Postgres pg_stat_activity wait_event, pg_locks; MySQL performance_schema/InnoDB status.

Industry examples. LMAX Disruptor (single writer, lock-free ring buffer) for trading; Java's LongAdder born from this; Instagram/Twitter counters sharded; Kafka and Redis single-threaded event loops avoid locks by design (Redis executes commands on one thread).

Decision gravity. Choosing a concurrency model (shared state with locks vs single-writer/actors) is a deep design choice, hard to change later; reducing lock scope inside code is cheap and reversible.

Everyday analogy. A single toilet in an office: more employees do not make the queue shorter; more toilets (finer granularity) do.

Common interview traps.

  • Adding threads to a lock-bound system.
  • Holding a lock across network or disk I/O.
  • A single global counter or row updated by every request.
  • Inconsistent lock ordering (deadlock).

notes.title: GC pauses and memory pressure
notes.html:
Garbage collection (GC) reclaims unused memory automatically, but some phases stop the application (stop-the-world, STW). Long pauses show up as latency spikes, timeouts, and failed health checks.

Why it matters at senior level: a 3-second pause makes a node look dead (missed heartbeats, lock lease expiry, failover, load balancer ejection), which can cascade into split brain or retry storms.

Rough JVM picture (confirm per version):

  • Young generation collections are frequent and short (milliseconds).
  • Old generation / full GC can be long with big heaps and the older collectors (seconds).
  • G1 (default since Java 9) targets a pause goal (-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200); ZGC and Shenandoah aim for sub-millisecond to few-millisecond pauses largely independent of heap size (ZGC generational mode added in newer JDKs). Pick a modern collector for latency-sensitive services.
  • Allocation rate drives GC frequency: allocating 1 GB/s with a 2 GB young gen means a young GC every couple of seconds.

Common causes and fixes:

  • High allocation rate: reduce garbage (avoid boxing, string concatenation in loops, large temporary lists, JSON parsing copies); reuse buffers; object pools only when profiling proves it.
  • Heap too small (constant GC) or too large with old collector (long full GC).
  • Memory leak: unbounded cache/static map/listener never removed: the old generation fills, full GCs become back-to-back, throughput collapses ("GC death spiral" where the JVM spends >98% time in GC and throws OutOfMemoryError: GC overhead limit exceeded).
  • Large humongous allocations in G1 (objects over half a region).
  • Container limits: JVM heap + metaspace + threads + native memory exceed the pod's memory limit and the OOM killer ends the process (use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70; confirm flags for your JDK).
  • Safepoint pauses and swap activity (never swap a JVM).
# JVM flags often used for a latency-sensitive service (illustrative, tune with measurements)
java -XX:+UseZGC -Xms4g -Xmx4g -XX:+AlwaysPreTouch \
     -Xlog:gc*:file=/var/log/gc.log:time,uptime \
     -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -jar app.jar

Detection. GC logs (-Xlog:gc*), JFR, metrics like jvm_gc_pause_seconds, heap usage after GC trending upward (leak), p99 latency spikes aligned with GC events; heap dumps (Eclipse MAT) to find leaks.

Android angle. ART's GC is concurrent but allocation-heavy code in onDraw, scrolling lists or per-frame objects causes jank (dropped frames, 16 ms budget at 60 Hz). Fixes: avoid allocations in hot UI paths, reuse objects, use RecyclerView view recycling, profile with Android Studio Memory Profiler, watch for leaked Activities (static references, listeners).

Worked example. Service with a 16 GB heap on old Parallel GC sees a 4 s full GC every 30 minutes; the load balancer health check times out at 3 s and removes the node, then all nodes do it around the same time. Moving to G1/ZGC with a 6 GB heap and fixing a 2 KB-per-request garbage source reduces pauses to under 20 ms.

Industry examples. Discord (Go to Rust for Read States service due to GC spikes), Twitter (tuning JVM, Finagle), LinkedIn, Netflix (JVM tuning with G1/ZGC), Cassandra (historically GC-sensitive, community moved to G1/ZGC), Elasticsearch (heap capped near 30 GB to keep compressed object pointers).

Decision gravity. Collector choice and heap sizing are reversible flags. Moving language/runtime (JVM to Rust/C++) is a one-way door chosen only for extreme latency or memory needs. Make sure heartbeat timeouts exceed realistic pauses.

Everyday analogy. A restaurant that stops serving for a few minutes while staff clear all tables at once: customers notice, and the longer the break, the angrier they are.

Common interview traps.

  • "Just give it more heap": larger heap with a pausing collector means longer pauses.
  • Treating GC as a magic detail instead of a source of latency spikes and false failure detection.
  • Setting health-check or lease timeouts shorter than the worst GC pause.

notes.title: Other common anti-patterns and a checklist
notes.html:
Short list worth recognising:

Anti-pattern Symptom Fix
Missing index / full table scan Query time grows with table size, DB CPU high EXPLAIN ANALYZE, add the right composite index
Over-fetching (SELECT *, huge payloads) High bandwidth, memory Select needed columns, paginate, compress
Offset pagination on big tables Page 10,000 is slow (OFFSET 1000000) Keyset (seek) pagination WHERE id > :last ORDER BY id LIMIT 50
Synchronous work in the request path High latency tails Move email, thumbnails, analytics to async queue
Connection per request TLS and connection setup cost, DB max connections Connection pools, keep-alive, HTTP/2, PgBouncer
Hot partition / hot key One shard at 100%, others idle Better key, salting, split hot key, local cache
Serial processing of independent work Latency = sum Parallelise within limits
No caching of expensive pure results Repeated identical computation Cache with TTL, invalidate carefully
Premature or wrong microservices Chatty calls, distributed monolith Fewer, domain-aligned services
Logging/serialization on the hot path CPU in JSON/log frameworks Async logging, sampling, binary formats

Quick checklist for design reviews:

  1. Any loop that makes a DB or network call per item?
  2. Any queue, pool, cache or result set without a bound?
  3. Any hot key, hot row or single global lock?
  4. Do all remote calls have timeouts, and are retries jittered and budgeted?
  5. What happens when the cache is cold or a key expires?
  6. What are GC/pause and heartbeat timeouts relative to each other?
  7. Which metrics (p99, queue depth, lock wait, GC pause) will tell us?

Worked example. Keyset vs offset pagination: OFFSET 1,000,000 LIMIT 50 makes Postgres read and discard 1M rows (hundreds of ms to seconds), while WHERE id > 1000000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 using the primary key index reads 50 rows (under a millisecond).

Industry examples. Slack, Stripe and GitHub APIs use cursor-based pagination for exactly this reason; Amazon DynamoDB hot-partition guidance; Instagram's early use of PgBouncer.

Common interview traps.

  • Listing anti-patterns without how you would detect them.
  • Fixing the one you know (e.g. caching) while the bottleneck is elsewhere.
  • Not stating the metric that proves the fix worked.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Measure first; find the bottleneck resource; fix the biggest one; re-measure (Amdahl: small parts of the time cannot give big wins).
  • N+1: one query per item. Use joins, batched IN queries, DataLoader, and assert query counts.
  • Chatty services: many small calls add latency and multiply failure odds. Batch, parallelise, aggregate (BFF), align boundaries to data.
  • Thundering herd and cache stampede: single flight, locks/leases, stale-while-revalidate, TTL jitter, warm caches; also retry and reconnect storms.
  • Unbounded queues, pools, caches and result sets turn overload into OOM and huge latency. Bound everything and choose an overflow policy.
  • Lock contention: low CPU but poor throughput. Shorten critical sections, shard, use lock-free or single-writer designs; beware hot DB rows and keyset vs offset pagination.
  • GC pauses cause latency spikes and false failure detection; pick a suitable collector, reduce allocation, fix leaks, and keep timeouts above worst-case pauses.
